result.summary: Flushes buffered block and undo data explicitly before the writer goes out of scope, catching write exceptions, logging them, and triggering a fatal node shutdown. In `BufferedWriter::flush()`, clears pending bytes before writing to prevent the destructor from re-attempting a failed write during exception unwinding. Adds an `Assume` in the destructor to ensure callers flush explicitly.
result.problem: When disk writes fail (such as on a full filesystem), `AutoFile::write_buffer()` throws an exception. Because `BufferedWriter`'s destructor is implicitly non-throwing, an unhandled flush exception in the destructor invokes `std::terminate` instead of shutting down gracefully. Furthermore, failed flushes left pending bytes in the buffer, causing the destructor to throw a second time while unwinding.
evidence: Author description: "fwrite() can report fewer bytes written than requested after a local storage error, e.g., if the filesystem fills up while a block is being written (my 1 TB benchmarking servers have recently been filling up, so I've been seeing these failures more often)."
PR description identifies the bug as a regression introduced in #31551.
result.changed_since_previous: Rather than making `BufferedWriter::flush()` catch exceptions and return a boolean, `flush()` continues to throw; `BlockManager` catches `std::runtime_error` during block and undo writes and triggers fatal node shutdown rather than relying on `Assert()`.
result.card: Handles block and undo write errors explicitly so that filesystem failures (such as running out of disk space) trigger a clean fatal shutdown with diagnostic logs instead of crashing via std::terminate. In BufferedWriter, pending bytes are cleared before writing to prevent destructor retries during exception unwinding, and an Assume check detects unflushed buffers on destruction. This fixes a regression from #31551 observed when running out of disk space during benchmarks.

risk.why: Flaws in block serialization error handling or buffer flushing could cause corrupted block files or unexpected node terminations during block storage operations.
